endorsements.title: A multimodal, risk-stratified framework for AI-driven early risk prediction and personalised prevention in obesity
endorsements.quote: (ii) Alert fatigue and cognitive load. JITAI nudges and tier-escalation alerts must be governed by an explicit alert budget, batched daily summaries for Tier-C patients, and threshold-based suppression for spurious deviations—without this, clinician trust collapses regardless of model performance ( Hassan et al., 2024 ; Cangelosi et al., 2025 ).

commentary.bottom_line: Four guidance and framework documents endorse automatic drift and anomaly notifications to responsible staff, but no supplied study tests whether such notifications lead to earlier detection or fewer patient harms. Health systems adopting this practice would be acting on expert consensus and regulatory examples rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied evidence tests automatic drift or anomaly notifications, and no study documents how often unnoticed degradation occurs. The four endorsements come from two guidelines, one assurance framework, and one commentary. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not raise certainty, so the effect of this practice on detection time or patient outcomes remains unmeasured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes an example in which performance is calculated automatically every 6 months and an e-mail goes to the site administrator and sponsor when results fall outside the expected range. This draft language describes a practice without mandating it. CHAI and FUTURE-AI frame notification as a should-level expectation.

The obesity-prediction commentary warns that alerts without an explicit alert budget, batched summaries, and threshold-based suppression may erode clinician trust. That concern concerns patient-level alerts, but the same design question applies to drift notifications sent to administrators. No supplied study measures notification burden, response rates, or fidelity in real operational settings.

The FDA example suggests a low-frequency design, with checks every 6 months and a single e-mail, which would place modest demands on staff. A 6-month interval may miss faster drift, however. No supplied evidence reports the cost, staffing, or response workflow needed to act on notifications once they arrive.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare deployments with and without automatic drift and anomaly notifications and measure time from performance change to detection, the share of alerts that prompt action, false-alarm rates, and downstream patient outcomes. They should also examine how monitoring frequency and alert thresholds affect alert fatigue among the staff who receive them.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Drift that affects only a subgroup may not trigger notifications built on aggregate performance, and without subgroup-level evidence health systems cannot know whether these alerts would detect degradation concentrated in underserved patients.
